passages.original: Propter igitur accidens captiones sunt,quando similiter quodcunque existimabitur rei et accidenti inesse: nam quia multa eidem accidunt, non est necesse omnibus prædicatis et ei de quo prædicantur, illa omnia inesse. Nam omnia sicerunt eadem,quemadmodum sophistae dicunt:ut si Coriscus est alter ab homine,ipse est alter a se, est enim homo; aut si a Socrate alter,Socrates autem homo ab homine alterum dicunt esse confessum, eo quod accidit (a quo dixit alterum esse) hunc esse hominem.Propter id autem quod hoc quidem simpliciter, illud autem aliquo modo, et non praecipue, quando quod in parte dicitur, ut simpliciter dictum sumitur, ut si non ens est opinabile quod non ens est;
passages.english: Deceptions, then, that arise from the accident occur whenever it is supposed that any attribute belongs in the same way to the thing and to its accident: for since many things are accidents of the same thing, it is not necessary that all of them belong to all the predicates and to that of which they are predicated. For then all things would be the same, as the sophists say: for example, if Coriscus is other than man, he is other than himself, for he is a man; or if he is other than Socrates, and Socrates is a man, they say [the opponent] has admitted that he is other than man, because it happens that the one from whom he said [Coriscus] was other is a man. Deceptions arise from the fact that this is said simply and that in some respect, and not strictly, when what is said in part is taken as if it were said simply: for example, if what is not is an object of opinion, [the argument concludes] that what is not is;
passages.notes: 'sicerunt' read as 'sic erunt' ('would then be'). The final clause ('quod non ens est') is elliptical; the sense, supported by the following context, is that what is not 'is' (exists) because it is an object of opinion. 'Ab homine alterum' taken as 'other than man'; 'confessum' refers to the respondent's admission.

passages.original: Et syllogismus contentiosus et sophisticus, unus quidem est apparens syllogismus, cirea ea de quibus dialectica tentativa est,quamvis vera sit conclusio : nam ejus quod est propter quid, hallucinatorius est,et quæcunque (cum non sint( secundum cujusque disciplinam captiosae ratiocinationes,videntur esse secundum artem.Nam pseudographiae non contentiosae (secundum enim ea quae sub arte sunt, captiosae sunt ratrocinationes) neque si aliqua est pseudographia circa verum, ut Hippocratis quadratura quae per lunulas ; sed ut Brysso quadravit circulum,et tametsi quadraretur circulus,quia tamen non secundum rem,ideo sophisticus ; quare et qui de his quidem apparens syllogismus, contentiosa est oratio : nam apparens est secundum rem,quare fallax et injusta.Quemadmodum enim ea (quae in certamineest) injuria quamdam speciem habet et est quaedam injusta pugua, sic in contradictione injusta pugna contentiosa est, nam et illic qui omnino vincere volunt,omnia tentant, et hic qui contentiosi sunt.
passages.english: And a contentious and sophistical syllogism is, in one sense, an apparent syllogism about those matters with which tentative dialectic is concerned, even if the conclusion is true; for it is deceptive about the reason why. [It is] also whatever fallacious reasonings, while not being in accordance with the discipline of each [subject], seem to be in accordance with the art. For false diagrams are not contentious (for the fallacious reasonings are in accordance with the things that fall under the art), nor is it so if there is some false diagram concerning what is true, such as Hippocrates' squaring by means of lunes; but the way Bryson squared the circle, even if the circle were squared, still, because [it was] not in accordance with the subject matter, is for that reason sophistical. Therefore both the apparent syllogism about these things is a contentious argument, and [the syllogism] that is apparent in accordance with the subject matter [is contentious], so that it is fallacious and unjust. For just as unfairness in a contest has a certain form and is a kind of unjust fighting, so in disputation contentiousness is unjust fighting; for there too those who want to win at all costs try everything, and here so do those who are contentious.
passages.notes: Scanning errors silently corrected: 'cirea' (circa), 'ratrocinationes' (ratiocinationes), 'pugua' (pugna), 'certamineest' (certamine est). The Latin of the clause 'quare et qui de his quidem apparens syllogismus... nam apparens est secundum rem' is compressed and probably faulty in this text; translated on the sense that both the merely apparent syllogism and the one that is apparently about the subject matter count as contentious. 'Hallucinatorius' rendered 'deceptive'. 'Pseudographia' rendered 'false diagram' (geometrical false proof). 'Brysso' is taken as Bryson, the sophist who squared the circle.
